story: SeL4: OS with formal correctness + security proof
text: [VIDEO] The implementation is correct against this abstract specification ... so bug-free, etc. The implications, there's many of them, but just a few obvious ones: it's not possible for this kernel to have a buffer overflow; it cannot - it provably does not use uninitialized variables or dereference null pointers, there's no stack smashing, you can't have code injection, there's no return oriented programming. Any of that stuff is just not possible - provably. So that's nice!

story: Manux – A free Linux-compatible OS designed to withstand attacks in userspace
text: Spent a while on the weekend reading about the seL4 kernel, which uses capability based security and has end to end mathematical proofs of correctness on the compiler and underlying kernel. Its predecessors are used in Apple's A7 and Qualcomm's chips. Watching [VIDEO] and it says that it's mathematically impossible for seL4 to suffer from things such as buffer overflows. I'm faaaaaar out of my field here... but this sounds as like a far better improvement in security compared to running things in a chroot. Apart from it being really new (there's just a kernel with a C compiler), would this be a good route to head down for improving security? Why aren't we writing a linux port on this?
